steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Fine-tuned language models (LMs) are widely and successfully used, but they have several drawbacks. They need significant compute resources for training, large amounts of labelled data, and separate training and storage for every downstream task. Prompting language models solves some of these problems, but designing prompts that give optimal performance for a given downstream application is hard. There has been significant progress on methods for automatic prompt engineering. One of these methods for automatically optimizing prompts is soft-prompt tuning. It is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method that trains a small set of prompt-token embeddings, which are given together with the standard natural language input. For various LLMs it has been shown that soft-prompt tuning matches, or nearly matches, fine-tuning performance for different tasks such as classification, summarization, and question-answering.

On the other hand, it is well-documented that popular LMs show potentially harmful biases, and this is quite common. Bias quantification has recently gotten a lot of attention from the research community. LLM applications keep expanding fast, so it is imperative to develop comprehensive analytical frameworks that measure the social biases that these models learned or inherited.

- Our approach
  - soft-prompt tuning for bias evaluation of LLMs: OPT, LLaMA
  - optimized soft-prompts condition models for sentiment analysis; fairness (bias) metrics measured on it
  - efficient in parameters tuned; no human bias injected through manual prompt design
  - fine-grained analysis, overall understanding of bias w.r.t. sensitive attributes, across protected groups
- Contributions
  - first application of soft-prompt tuning for fairness evaluation; effective and efficient
  - OPT, LLaMA: measurable biases across protected groups (age, sexuality, disability); consistent across model size, type, prompt-tuning dataset
  - metrics: positive and negative false-positive rate gaps; compatible with other fairness measures (comprehensive fairness suite from prior work)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Fine-tuned language models (LMs) are widely and successfully used, but they have several drawbacks. They need significant compute resources for training, large amounts of labelled data, and separate training and storage for every downstream task. Prompting language models solves some of these problems, but designing prompts that give optimal performance for a given downstream application is hard. There has been significant progress on methods for automatic prompt engineering. One of these methods for automatically optimizing prompts is soft-prompt tuning. It is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method that trains a small set of prompt-token embeddings, which are given together with the standard natural language input. For various LLMs it has been shown that soft-prompt tuning matches, or nearly matches, fine-tuning performance for different tasks such as classification, summarization, and question-answering.

On the other hand, it is well-documented that popular LMs show potentially harmful biases, and this is quite common. Bias quantification has recently gotten a lot of attention from the research community. LLM applications keep expanding fast, so it is imperative to develop comprehensive analytical frameworks that measure the social biases that these models learned or inherited.

In this paper we evaluate how useful soft-prompt tuning is for evaluating bias in LLMs, including OPT and LLaMA language models. More specifically, our approach uses optimized soft-prompts to condition the models toward completing sentiment analysis tasks, and then fairness (bias) metrics are measured on these tasks. The method is efficient in terms of the number of parameters tuned, and another advantage of soft-prompt tuning is that it does not inject any human bias through manual prompt design. The experiments show that prompt-tuning makes it possible to do fine-grained analysis and get an overall understanding of an LLM's bias with respect to sensitive attributes and across protected groups. The contributions of this paper are:

- • As far as we know, this is the first time soft-prompt tuning is applied to fairness evaluation. We show that the approach is an effective and efficient approach for this evaluation.

- • We show that LLMs such as OPT and LLaMA have measurable biases across protected groups within the sensitive attributes of age, sexuality, and disability. These biases are also generally consistent across model size, type, and prompt-tuning dataset.

- • We explore the bias metrics of positive and negative false-positive rate gaps. But the approach is also compatible with other fairness measures, including the comprehensive fairness suite proposed in prior work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Despite widespread and successful use, fine-tuned language models (LMs) have several drawbacks. These include requiring significant compute resources for training, large quantities of labelled data, and separate training and storage for each downstream task [1,2]. Language model prompting addresses some of these downsides, but designing prompts that induce optimal performance for a given downstream application is challenging [3,4]. Significant progress has been made in automatic prompt engineering methods. One such method for automatic prompt optimization is soft-prompt tuning, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method that trains a small set of prompt-token embeddings provided along with the standard natural language input. For various LLMs, soft-prompt tuning has been shown to match, or nearly match, fine-tuning performance on tasks such as classification, summarization, and question-answering [5,6].

On the other hand, the potentially harmful biases exhibited by popular LMs are well-documented [7,8,9,10] and quite common. Bias quantification has recently gained substantial attention from the research community [11,12]. As LLM applications continue to expand rapidly, developing comprehensive analytical frameworks to measure the learned or inherited social biases of such models is imperative.

In this paper, we evaluate the utility of soft-prompt tuning for bias evaluation of LLMs, including OPT [13] and LLaMA language models [14]. More specifically, our approach leverages optimized soft-prompts to condition models toward the completion of sentiment analysis tasks, on which fairness (bias) metrics are subsequently measured. Besides the method's efficiency in terms of the number of parameters tuned, another advantage of soft-prompt tuning is that it eliminates any injection of human bias through manual prompt design. The experiments demonstrate that prompt-tuning enables fine-grained analysis and an overall understanding of an LLM's bias with respect to sensitive attributes and across protected groups. This paper's contributions are as follows:

- • To our knowledge, this is the first application of soft-prompt tuning for fairness evaluation. We demonstrate that it constitutes an effective and efficient approach for such evaluation.

- • We show that LLMs such as OPT and LLaMA exhibit measurable biases across protected groups within the sensitive attributes of age, sexuality, and disability. Furthermore, these biases are generally consistent across model size, type, and prompt-tuning dataset.

- • We explore the bias metrics of positive and negative false-positive rate gaps. However, the approach is compatible with other fairness measures, including the comprehensive fairness suite proposed in [15].
